title: 1 Kings 19:19–21
context: Elijah finds Elisha the son of Shaphat plowing with twelve yoke of oxen and throws his mantle on him, a gesture commonly understood as a call to succeed him. Elisha asks to kiss his father and mother first, and Elijah’s reply, Go back again; for what have I done to you, is understood in different ways, as permission, as a test, or as a reminder of the seriousness of the call. Elisha then slaughters his oxen, cooks them with the oxen’s equipment, feeds the people, and follows Elijah as his servant. Interpreters commonly compare this scene with Jesus’ words about the plow and looking back (Luke 9:61–62), though the stories are not identical. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the passage as shared ground about wholehearted response to God’s call and the continuation of prophetic ministry.

verses.text: So he departed from there and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth. Elijah went over to him and put his mantle on him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah finding Elisha plowing with twelve yoke of oxen and throwing his mantle on him. The call comes in the middle of ordinary work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s call through Elijah as an effectual summons to prophetic service. Readers in both traditions commonly read the mantle as a sign of succession (compare 2 Kings 2:13).

verses.text: Elisha left the oxen and ran after Elijah, and said, “Let me please kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.” He said to him, “Go back again; for what have I done to you?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elisha running after Elijah and asking to kiss his parents before following. His response is eager yet tied to family.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Elijah’s reply as testing Elisha’s commitment, though interpreters differ on its tone. Both traditions commonly compare the scene with Jesus’ words about the plow (Luke 9:61–62).

verses.text: He returned from following him, and took the yoke of oxen, killed them, and boiled their meat with the oxen’s equipment, and gave to the people; and they ate. Then he arose, and went after Elijah, and served him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elisha slaughtering his oxen, cooking them with the oxen’s equipment, feeding the people, and following Elijah. He leaves his old life decisively.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his full commitment as the fruit of God’s call (compare Mark 10:29). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a picture of wholehearted discipleship and service.
